brief.topic: Why Popular People Appear More Often in Your Sample

s01: Pick a person at random, or pick a random end of a friendship.
Those are different ways to sample the same people.
Here is a tiny network.
One person has four friends.
Each of the other four people has just one.
There are five people and eight friendship ends.
Sampling people equally gives an average friend count of eight divided by five.
One point six.
Now put a name on each end of every friendship.
The central person's name appears four times.
Each other name appears once.
Choose one of these eight names equally.
Four names lead to someone with four friends.
Four lead to someone with one.
The average is twenty divided by eight: two point five.
The popular person occupies more places in this sample.
For any undirected network with an edge, this average is the sum of squared degrees divided by the sum of degrees.
It is at least the ordinary average degree, because degree variance cannot be negative.
If everyone has the same number of friends, the averages agree.
This is one precise form of the friendship paradox.
It does not say every person's friends are more popular.
It says our sampling route changes who we are likely to encounter.

scenes.narration:
Pick a person at random, or pick a random end of a friendship. Those are different ways to sample the same people.

Here is a tiny network. One person has four friends. Each of the other four people has just one. There are five people and eight friendship ends.

Sampling people equally gives an average friend count of eight divided by five. One point six.

Now put a name on each end of every friendship. The central person's name appears four times. Each other name appears once. Choose one of these eight names equally.

Four names lead to someone with four friends. Four lead to someone with one. The average is twenty divided by eight: two point five. The popular person occupies more places in this sample.

For any undirected network with an edge, this average is the sum of squared degrees divided by the sum of degrees. It is at least the ordinary average degree, because degree variance cannot be negative.

If everyone has the same number of friends, the averages agree. This is one precise form of the friendship paradox. It does not say every person's friends are more popular. It says our sampling route changes who we are likely to encounter.
